title: The Rabbit and the Tar Wolf
subtitle: A printed Cherokee animal story about a stolen drink

tarwolf.author: James Mooney
tarwolf.locator: Myth 21 · THE RABBIT AND THE TAR WOLF, normalized characters 451-1423
tarwolf.excerpt: They noticed that the Rabbit kept sleek and lively, although it was still dry weather and the water was getting low in the well. They said, "That tricky Rabbit steals our water at night," so they made a wolf of pine gum and tar and set it up by the well to scare the thief. That night the Rabbit came, as he had been coming every night, to drink enough to last him all next day. He saw the queer black thing by the well and said, "Who's there?" but the tar wolf said nothing. He came nearer, but the wolf never moved, so he grew braver and said, "Get out of my way or I'll strike you." Still the wolf never moved and the Rabbit came up and struck it with his paw, but the gum held his foot and it stuck fast. Now he was angry and said, "Let me go or I'll kick you." Still the wolf said nothing. Then the Rabbit struck again with his hind foot, so hard that it was caught in the gum and he could not move, and there he stuck until the animals came for water in the morning.
tarwolf.note: Verbatim English text from Mooney's 1902 collection. Keep the specific numbered story and its East Cherokee/recorded-source context attached.

narrativeBlocks.title: The wolf made of tar
narrativeBlocks.body: The other animals, tired of the Rabbit's tricks, make a wolf out of tar and set it in his path — a trap made of the trickster's own habits.

narrativeBlocks.title: A stranger who won't move
narrativeBlocks.body: The Rabbit greets the tar-wolf; it doesn't answer. He hits it — his paw sticks. He hits again — another paw sticks. Soon the trickster is stuck fast, all four paws and his head, helpless.

narrativeBlocks.title: Tricked into the briars
narrativeBlocks.body: Caught, he pleads with his captors: 'Throw me anywhere but the briar-patch!' They take the bait — hurl him into the briars, and the Rabbit is free and laughing, for the briar-patch is his home.

narrativeBlocks.title: The ancestor of Br'er Rabbit
narrativeBlocks.body: This Cherokee tale is the ancestor of the famous Br'er Rabbit tar-baby story — printed in the Cherokee Advocate in the 1840s, generations before the version the wider world knows.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why the Cherokee tar-wolf matters
narrativeBlocks.body: The trickster stuck to a tar-figure and freed by a feigned plea is one of America's great story-patterns — and this collection shows it in its Cherokee form, on Cherokee terms.
